chunks: What an eye diagram shows. The question: What is an eye digram? What does it represent?
An eye diagram is a picture made by laying every bit of a long data stream on top of each other, all lined up to the same one-bit time slot.
The traces cross and bunch into a shape like an eye. The open space in the middle is where the receiver can safely read a 1 or a 0. A big, clear opening means plenty of margin.
Take a long strip of paper with the data waveform drawn on it, cut it into pieces exactly one bit long, and stack them on a light table.
Where the pieces agree, the lines are sharp. Where they differ, they spread. The clear gap left in the middle is the eye.
It shows the worst case among all the bits, not the average.
A serial NRZ waveform with the clock that marks each bit boundary. Cut at every clock edge and stack the pieces: those pieces are the traces of the eye.
Bit time (unit interval, UI): how long one bit lasts. At 10 Gb/s that is 100 picoseconds. Eye height: how much voltage separates a 1 from a 0 at the best sampling moment.
Eye width: how much time the receiver has to sample, around that moment.
Inter-symbol interference (ISI): each bit's waveform getting smeared by the bits before it, because the channel has memory.
Jitter: edges arriving early or late, which blurs the crossings sideways ("Jitter").
At 10 Gb/s each bit lasts 100 picoseconds. Suppose a perfect signal swings 800 millivolts between its 0 and 1 levels.
The ideal eye is 800 millivolts tall and 100 picoseconds wide. Now a lossy cable smears the bits.
ISI closes the eye by 200 millivolts in total, part from the top and part from the bottom, leaving 600 millivolts of height.
Jitter makes the crossings fuzzy and takes 20 picoseconds from the width, leaving 80 picoseconds.
That is the whole idea: one picture of all the bits, with the opening showing the margin.
"An eye diagram overlays all the bits of a serial data stream onto one unit interval, usually by triggering a scope from the clock with persistence.
The open area in the middle is where the receiver can sample safely.
Eye height shows voltage margin after ISI and noise, eye width shows timing margin, UI minus jitter, and the crossings and trace thickness show duty cycle, jitter and noise.
A big clean opening means a low bit error rate; a closed eye means errors."
